# OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet Source: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html Retrieved: 2026-10-11 Author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series Team

## Introduction Authentication is the process of verifying that an individual, entity, or website is who they claim to be. Authentication in the context of web applications is commonly performed by submitting a username or ID and one or more items of private information that only a given user should know. Session management is a process by which a server maintains the state of a user's authentication so that the user may continue to use the system without re-authenticating.

## Password Storage Requirements Passwords must never be stored in plaintext. Appropriate one-way hashing using modern adaptive algorithms must be used. Recommended algorithms ordered by preference: 1. **Argon2id** — memory-hard, time-cost, and parallelism parameters must be configured. Use a minimum of 64 MB memory, 3 iterations, and 4 parallel threads for interactive logins. 2. **bcrypt** — cost factor of at least 10 (recommend 12+) to protect against brute-force attacks. 3. **scrypt** — requi

factor of at least 10 (recommend 12+) to protect against brute-force attacks. 3. **scrypt** — requires careful tuning of N, r, and p parameters. N=32768, r=8, p=1 is a reasonable starting point. 4. **PBKDF2** — use PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with at least 600,000 iterations for passwords. Never use MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, or any raw (unsalted) hash for password storage. These are designed for speed, not security, and are trivially vulnerable to dictionary attacks and rainbow tables.

## Password Strength Requirements Enforce the following minimum password policy: - Minimum 12 characters in length. - Allow all printable ASCII characters plus Unicode. - Do NOT enforce composition rules (uppercase/lowercase/digit/special) — length matters more. - Check passwords against a breach corpus such as HaveIBeenPwned or the NIST SP 800-63B word list. - Implement a password strength meter to encourage strong choices rather than only enforcing minimum rules.

## Hardcoded Credentials in Source Code Hardcoding passwords, API keys, tokens, or secrets directly in source code is a critical security failure corresponding to CWE-798 (Use of Hard-coded Credentials) and OWASP A07:2021. ### Vulnerable Pattern (Python) python

# NEVER hardcode credentials DB_PASSWORD = "SuperSecret123!" # Hardcoded secret — OWASP A07 API_KEY = "sk-live-abc123secret" # Hardcoded API key — CWE-798 ### Secure Pattern (Python) import os DB_PASSWORD = os.getenv("DB_PASSWORD") API_KEY = os.getenv("API_KEY") if not DB_PASSWORD or not API_KEY: raise RuntimeError("Required secrets not configured in environment variables.") ### Vulnerable Pattern (Java) // NEVER hardcode credentials in Java source files private static final String API_SECRET =

(Java) // NEVER hardcode credentials in Java source files private static final String API_SECRET = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"; // Exposed to decompilers private static final String DB_PASS = "RootAdmin2026!"; ### Secure Pattern (Java) // Load secrets from environment variables or a secrets manager private static final String API_SECRET = System.getenv("API_SECRET"); private static final String DB_PASS = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"); Use AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, or equi
S = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"); Use AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, or equivalent to manage production credentials externally.

## Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) Implement MFA for all accounts with elevated privileges. TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password, RFC 6238) using authenticator apps (e.g. Google Authenticator, Authy) is strongly recommended. Hardware security keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) provide the strongest protection against phishing.

## Brute Force Protection - Implement account lockout after 5–10 consecutive failed login attempts. - Use exponential back-off or CAPTCHA after repeated failures. - Log and alert on suspicious login patterns. - Never reveal whether a username exists via differential error messages: always return "Invalid username or password."

## Secure Session Management - Generate session IDs with a cryptographically secure random source of at least 128 bits of entropy. - Regenerate session ID on privilege level change (e.g., after successful login). - Set Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Strict attributes on session cookies. - Invalidate sessions on server-side upon logout. - Set appropriate session timeout (idle and absolute).

## Authentication Error Messages Never differentiate between invalid username and invalid password in error messages. Always use a generic message: "Invalid credentials." This prevents user enumeration attacks.

text: ## Introduction Access control (or authorization) enforces policy such that users cannot act outside of their intended permissions. Failures typically lead to unauthorized information disclosure, modification, destruction of data, or performing a business function outside the user's limits.

# OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet Source: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cryptographic_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html Retrieved: 2026-10-11 Author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series Team

## Introduction The purpose of this cheat sheet is to provide developers with a simple checklist to protect sensitive data at rest and ensure proper cryptographic controls are implemented across their applications.

section: Broken and Insecure Algorithms to Avoid
text: ## Broken and Insecure Algorithms to Avoid Do not use legacy, collision-vulnerable, or deprecated cryptographic algorithms: - **Broken Hashing Algorithms:** MD5, SHA-1, MD4, RIPEMD. Practical collision attacks exist against MD5 and SHA-1 that allow attackers to forge digital signatures and generate identical hashes for different contents. - **Broken Symmetric Ciphers:** DES, Triple DES (3DES), RC4, Blowfish. - **Insecure Modes of Operation:** Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode must never be used bec

section: Broken and Insecure Algorithms to Avoid
text: , Blowfish. - **Insecure Modes of Operation:** Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode must never be used because identical plaintext blocks encrypt to identical ciphertext blocks, preserving structural data patterns.

## Recommended Strong Cryptographic Algorithms - **Cryptographic Hashes (Integrity & Signatures):** SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, or SHA-3 family. - **Password Storage:** Never use plain cryptographic hashes (like SHA-256 alone) for passwords. Always use adaptive, memory-hard key derivation functions: Argon2id (recommended), bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with high iteration counts (minimum 600,000 iterations for HMAC-SHA256). - **Symmetric Encryption:** AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) with 256-bit keys o
ions for HMAC-SHA256). - **Symmetric Encryption:** AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) with 256-bit keys or ChaCha20-Poly1305, providing authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD).

## Key Management and Secret Storage - Never hardcode cryptographic keys, secret tokens, or API passwords in source code. - Keys must be generated using cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generators (CSPRNG), such as Python's `secrets` module or Java's `SecureRandom`. - Secrets should be externalized into secure key management systems (e.g., AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) or system environment variables.
# OWASP Deserialization Cheat Sheet Source: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Deserialization_Cheat_Sheet.html Retrieved: 2026-10-11 Author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series Team

## Introduction Serialization is the process of translating data structures or object state into a format that can be stored or transmitted across a network and reconstructed later. Deserialization is the reverse process: extracting a data structure from a series of bytes. Insecure deserialization is a vulnerability where untrusted data is used to inflict a denial of service, execute arbitrary code, or bypass authentication.

## Python Deserialization Guidance Python's standard `pickle` module is explicitly not secure against erroneous or maliciously constructed data. The `pickle` protocol allows arbitrary Python objects to define `__reduce__` or `__reduce_ex__` methods, which direct the unpickler to invoke any callable with arbitrary arguments during deserialization. python

# VULNERABLE: data = pickle.loads(untrusted_stream) # Remote Code Execution vulnerability! Remediation: 1. Never unpickle untrusted data. 2. Use safe data exchange formats such as JSON, Protocol Buffers, or CBOR. 3. If YAML is used, always use `yaml.safe_load(data)` or `yaml.load(data, Loader=yaml.SafeLoader)`.

## Java Deserialization Guidance Java native serialization using `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` permits the deserialization of complex object graphs. Attackers construct "gadget chains"—sequences of classes already present on the application classpath (e.g., Apache Commons Collections, Spring Framework, Groovy)—that trigger arbitrary method execution during object reconstruction. // VULNERABLE: ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(untrustedInputStream); Object obj = ois.readObject();

ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(untrustedInputStream); Object obj = ois.readObject(); // RCE via gadget chains! Remediation: 1. Do not accept Java serialized objects from untrusted sources. 2. If serialized objects must be received, implement `ValidatingObjectInputStream` or use the Java 9+ serialization filtering API (`java.io.ObjectInputFilter`). 3. Migrate to JSON (Jackson, Gson) or Protocol Buffers.
# OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet Source: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html Retrieved: 2026-10-11 Author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series Team

## Introduction Input validation is performed to ensure only properly formed data enters the workflow of an information system, preventing malformed data from persisting in the database and triggering malfunction of various downstream components. Input validation must be applied at every tier of the application (client, server, and database layer). Server-side validation is mandatory — client-side validation is convenience only and can be trivially bypassed.

## Goals of Input Validation - Prevent injection attacks (SQLi, XSS, Command Injection, LDAP Injection, XML Injection). - Enforce business-rule constraints on data (type, length, format, range). - Reject unexpected, malicious, or malformed data before it reaches sensitive operations.

## Validation Strategies ### Allowlist (Whitelist) Validation — Preferred Approach Define and enforce exactly what is acceptable. Reject anything that does not match the allowlist. This is the strongest form of validation. import re def validate_username(username: str) -> bool: """Only allow alphanumeric and underscore, 3–32 chars.""" return bool(re.match(r'^[a-zA-Z0-9_]{3,32}$', username)) def validate_integer_range(value: str, min_val: int, max_val: int) -> int: """Strictly parse and range-che

lidate_integer_range(value: str, min_val: int, max_val: int) -> int: """Strictly parse and range-check an integer parameter.""" try: n = int(value) except (ValueError, TypeError): raise ValueError(f"Expected integer, got: {value!r}") if not (min_val <= n <= max_val): raise ValueError(f"Value {n} out of allowed range [{min_val}, {max_val}].") return n ### Denylist (Blacklist) Validation — Weak, Avoid Attempting to enumerate all dangerous inputs is fragile and easily bypassed through encoding tric

id Attempting to enumerate all dangerous inputs is fragile and easily bypassed through encoding tricks (URL encoding, HTML entity encoding, Unicode normalization). Only use denylist as an additional layer, never as a primary defense.

section: SQL Injection Prevention via Parameterized Queries
text: ## SQL Injection Prevention via Parameterized Queries All SQL queries must use parameterized queries (prepared statements) — never concatenate user data into query strings. ### Python — Parameterized Query python

# SAFE: parameterized with placeholder cursor.execute( "SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE username = %s AND active = %s", (username, True) ) ### Java — PreparedStatement // SAFE: parameterized PreparedStatement String sql = "SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE username = ? AND active = ?"; PreparedStatement ps = connection.prepareStatement(sql); ps.setString(1, username); ps.setBoolean(2, true); ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery(); Never use `Statement.executeQuery("SELECT ... WHERE username = '" + u
ultSet rs = ps.executeQuery(); Never use `Statement.executeQuery("SELECT ... WHERE username = '" + username + "'")`.

## OS Command Injection Prevention Never pass user-supplied data to shell-executing functions. If system commands are unavoidable, use argument array form without invoking a shell. ### Python — Unsafe vs Safe python
# VULNERABLE: shell=True interprets shell metacharacters import subprocess subprocess.Popen("ping -c 1 " + user_input, shell=True) # Command injection!

# SAFE: argument list, shell=False (default) subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", user_input], shell=False, timeout=5) ### Java — Unsafe vs Safe // VULNERABLE: passes string to shell Runtime.getRuntime().exec("nslookup " + userInput); // SAFE: argument array bypasses shell interpretation String[] cmd = {"nslookup", userInput}; Runtime.getRuntime().exec(cmd);

## Path Traversal Prevention Normalize and canonicalize file paths before use. Reject paths containing `..` sequences. import os from pathlib import Path SAFE_BASE = Path("/var/app/uploads").resolve() def safe_file_path(user_filename: str) -> Path: """Reject path traversal attempts.""" candidate = (SAFE_BASE / user_filename).resolve() if not str(candidate).startswith(str(SAFE_BASE)): raise ValueError("Path traversal detected.") return candidate

## Data Type and Length Validation Always validate data type and length before processing: - Strings: maximum length enforced; reject binary or non-printable characters where not expected. - Integers/Floats: parse strictly, enforce min/max range. - Email addresses: validate against RFC 5321 structure; never use regex alone as sole sanitization. - File uploads: validate MIME type server-side (not client-supplied Content-Type), check magic bytes, enforce maximum file size.

## Encoding and Escaping Validation does not replace proper output encoding. Always apply context-aware escaping at the point of output: - HTML context: HTML-entity encode (`<` → `<`, `>` → `>`, `"` → `"`). - SQL context: use parameterized queries (never manual escaping). - Shell context: avoid entirely; if unavoidable use `shlex.quote()` in Python. - URL context: percent-encode user data.

text: # OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet Source: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/OS_Command_Injection_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html Retrieved: 2026-10-11 Author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series Team

document_title: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet
text: ## Introduction Command injection is an attack in which the goal is execution of arbitrary commands on the host operating system via a vulnerable application. Command injection vulnerabilities occur when an application passes unsafe user supplied data (forms, cookies, HTTP headers etc.) to a system shell. In this attack, the attacker-supplied operating system commands are executed with the privileges of the vulnerable application.

document_title: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet
section: Primary Defense: Avoid Calling OS Commands Directly
text: ## Primary Defense: Avoid Calling OS Commands Directly The primary defense against command injection is to avoid calling external system commands directly whenever built-in API functions or programming language libraries exist. For example, instead of running `os.system("rm " + filename)` or `Runtime.getRuntime().exec("del " + filename)`, use language APIs like `os.remove(filename)` or Java's `Files.delete(path)`.

document_title: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet
section: Defense: Parameterization and Avoiding the System Shell
text: ## Defense: Parameterization and Avoiding the System Shell If an external command must be executed, never invoke it through a command shell (such as `/bin/sh`, `/bin/bash`, `cmd.exe`, or `powershell.exe`). ### Python Subprocess Guidance In Python: - Use `subprocess.run()` or `subprocess.Popen()`. - Pass arguments as a discrete list of strings rather than a concatenated string. - Keep `shell=False` (which is the default). python

document_title: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet
section: SAFE: Arguments are passed directly to execve without shell expansion
text: # SAFE: Arguments are passed directly to execve without shell expansion import subprocess result = subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "4", target_host], shell=False, capture_output=True, text=True) - NEVER set `shell=True` when handling user input. - NEVER use `os.system()` or `os.popen()` because they always invoke the system shell. ### Java ProcessBuilder Guidance In Java: - Use `ProcessBuilder` with an array or List of arguments: ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("ping", "-c", "4", targetHost

section: OWASP Top 10 - 2025 The Ten Most Critical Web Application Security Risks
text: # OWASP Top 10 - 2025 The Ten Most Critical Web Application Security Risks Source: https://top10.owasp.org/2025/ Retrieved: 2026-10-14 Author: OWASP Foundation

## A01:2025 - Broken Access Control Access control enforces policy such that users cannot act outside of their intended permissions. Retains the #1 position in the 2025 rankings. Access control failures typically lead to unauthorized information disclosure, modification, or destruction of data, or performing a business function outside the user's limits. In the 2025 edition, Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) and Open Redirects have been officially incorporated into Broken Access Control, recogn

rgery (SSRF) and Open Redirects have been officially incorporated into Broken Access Control, recognizing that forcing an application server to act as an unauthorized proxy or redirect to untrusted destinations represents an access control boundary violation. Common access control vulnerabilities include bypassing access control checks by modifying URLs, internal application state, or HTML forms; using custom API attack tools; permitting viewing or editing someone else's account by providing its

using custom API attack tools; permitting viewing or editing someone else's account by providing its unique identifier (Insecure Direct Object References - IDOR); missing access controls on sensitive HTTP methods (POST, PUT, DELETE); elevation of privilege (acting as an administrator without logging in); metadata manipulation (replaying or tampering with JWT tokens or cookie permissions); CORS misconfiguration permitting unauthorized API access; and SSRF attacks where attackers coerce server req

configuration permitting unauthorized API access; and SSRF attacks where attackers coerce server requests to internal backends, loopback interfaces, or cloud metadata endpoints. Prevention requires enforcing least privilege by default, denying access unless explicitly granted, centralizing authorization checks in controllers or gateway filters, disabling directory browsing, recording access control failures, and validating destination IP addresses/hostnames with strict allowlists for outbound re
l failures, and validating destination IP addresses/hostnames with strict allowlists for outbound requests.

## A02:2025 - Security Misconfiguration Security Misconfiguration climbed significantly to #2 in the 2025 edition, reflecting the widespread complexity of multi-cloud architectures, container orchestration, microservices, and modern CI/CD pipelines. Security misconfiguration happens when security controls are inaccurately defined, implemented, or maintained, or left at default settings. Common vulnerabilities include unhardened default configurations, enabled default accounts and passwords, unne

nerabilities include unhardened default configurations, enabled default accounts and passwords, unnecessary enabled ports, features, components, services, or sample pages, missing or misconfigured HTTP security headers (such as Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options), overly permissive Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) configurations, verbose error messages displaying detailed stack traces or internal database error codes, misconfigured cloud storage permis

isplaying detailed stack traces or internal database error codes, misconfigured cloud storage permissions (e.g., publicly readable AWS S3 buckets, exposed Azure blobs), unpatched software or outdated container base images, and insecure configuration files with debug modes left active in production. Prevention requires automated, repeatable hardening processes, deploying environments via Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with immutable configurations, removing unused features and frameworks, disallowi

ture as Code (IaC) with immutable configurations, removing unused features and frameworks, disallowing default credentials, reviewing cloud permissions continuously, sending security headers, and sanitizing error responses for external clients.

## A03:2025 - Software Supply Chain Failures A major new category for the 2025 edition, expanding and superseding the previous "Vulnerable and Outdated Components" category. Modern applications are heavily assembled from thousands of third-party open-source libraries, container registries, build plugins, and automated CI/CD distribution pipelines. Software Supply Chain Failures encompass risks introduced across the entire software development, delivery, and deployment lifecycle. Attack vectors i

roduced across the entire software development, delivery, and deployment lifecycle. Attack vectors include malicious or hijacked open-source packages in public repositories (such as npm, PyPI, Maven Central, or Docker Hub), typosquatting, dependency confusion where attackers publish malicious public packages with internal namespace names, compromised developer or maintainer accounts, malicious build-time script execution during package installation (e.g. postinstall hooks), compromised CI/CD pip

ld-time script execution during package installation (e.g. postinstall hooks), compromised CI/CD pipelines injecting unauthorized code into release binaries, lack of cryptographic package verification, and unpatched CVEs in nested transitive dependencies. Prevention requires generating and maintaining an active Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), conducting automated Software Composition Analysis (SCA) in CI/CD pipelines, pinning exact package versions with cryptographic hash verification (lockfi

SCA) in CI/CD pipelines, pinning exact package versions with cryptographic hash verification (lockfiles), using private artifact repositories with scoped namespaces to prevent dependency confusion, enforcing multi-factor authentication (MFA) and least privilege for CI/CD runners and package registries, signing build artifacts with digital signatures (Sigstore, Cosign), and continuously inventorying and patching dependencies.

## A04:2025 - Cryptographic Failures Cryptographic Failures (ranked #4 in 2025, previously known as Sensitive Data Exposure) focuses on flaws related to cryptography that expose sensitive data in transit, at rest, or during processing. Sensitive data includes passwords, credit card numbers, health records, personal identifiable information (PII), secret keys, and business secrets requiring enhanced protection under regulations like GDPR and PCI-DSS. Failures occur when sensitive data is transmit

d protection under regulations like GDPR and PCI-DSS. Failures occur when sensitive data is transmitted in clear text protocols (such as unencrypted HTTP, SMTP, or FTP), when broken or deprecated cryptographic algorithms are utilized (e.g., MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES, RC4), when default or hardcoded cryptographic keys are used, when weak random number generators (e.g., standard pseudo-random generators instead of CSPRNG) are used for key or token generation, when initialization vectors (IVs) are reus

instead of CSPRNG) are used for key or token generation, when initialization vectors (IVs) are reused in cipher modes like CBC or GCM, and when passwords are stored using weak hashes without salt and memory-hard work factors. Prevention requires classifying all data processed, stored, or transmitted, encrypting all data in transit with modern TLS (TLS 1.3), disabling legacy cryptographic suites, encrypting sensitive data at rest using authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM), managing keys throug

encrypting sensitive data at rest using authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM), managing keys through dedicated Hardware Security Modules (HSM) or secrets managers, and hashing passwords exclusively with adaptive, salted algorithms such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or PBKDF2.

## A05:2025 - Injection Injection flaws (ranked #5 in 2025) occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query. The attacker's hostile payload tricks the interpreter into executing unintended commands, evaluating code, or accessing and modifying database records without authorization. Injection encompasses SQL Injection, NoSQL Injection, OS Command Injection, Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) injection, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI

Relational Mapping (ORM) injection, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), and Expression Language (EL) injection. Primary vectors include concatenating user input directly into SQL statements (`SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ' + user`), passing unsanitized parameters into system shells (`subprocess.Popen(cmd, shell=True)`, `Runtime.getRuntime().exec()`), evaluating untrusted strings as code (`eval()`, `exec()`), and rendering user inputs directly in web templates w

ntrusted strings as code (`eval()`, `exec()`), and rendering user inputs directly in web templates without contextual output encoding. Prevention requires keeping untrusted data strictly separate from commands and queries: utilizing parameterized queries and prepared statements for all database operations, avoiding system shells and using argument arrays (`shell=False`), implementing strict allowlist input validation, using modern web frameworks with automatic contextual output encoding, and imp
ist input validation, using modern web frameworks with automatic contextual output encoding, and implementing Content Security Policy (CSP).

## A06:2025 - Insecure Design Insecure Design (ranked #6 in 2025) focuses on risks related to design and architectural flaws. Unlike implementation bugs, an insecure design cannot be fixed by a perfect implementation because the necessary security controls were never designed into the system. Insecure design encompasses missing or flawed business logic controls, lack of threat modeling, failure to isolate tenant boundaries in multi-tenant SaaS architectures, insecure state machines allowing step

isolate tenant boundaries in multi-tenant SaaS architectures, insecure state machines allowing steps in a checkout or approval workflow to be bypassed, credential recovery flows based on weak security questions, and lack of defense-in-depth architecture. Prevention requires adopting a Secure Development Lifecycle (SDL) with application security reviews, conducting threat modeling during the architecture phase (identifying STRIDE threats and abuse cases), establishing secure design patterns and

tecture phase (identifying STRIDE threats and abuse cases), establishing secure design patterns and reference architectures, segregating networks and services by trust boundaries, limiting resource consumption per tenant to prevent DoS, and integrating security user stories and acceptance criteria directly into project management.

## A07:2025 - Authentication Failures Authentication Failures (formerly Identification and Authentication Failures, ranked #7 in 2025) occur when mechanisms verifying user identity, managing sessions, or protecting credentials fail, permitting attackers to impersonate legitimate users or compromise accounts. Common vulnerabilities include allowing automated credential stuffing and brute force attacks without rate limiting or CAPTCHA, permitting weak or well-known passwords without complexity and

cks without rate limiting or CAPTCHA, permitting weak or well-known passwords without complexity and breach checking, storing passwords in plain text or using reversible encryption, weak or insecure password recovery mechanisms, exposing session tokens in URLs, failing to invalidate session IDs during logout or password changes, missing multi-factor authentication (MFA) on sensitive accounts, hardcoding credentials, tokens, or API keys directly in source code or repositories, and predictable ses

coding credentials, tokens, or API keys directly in source code or repositories, and predictable session token generation. Prevention requires enforcing Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), enforcing password strength and checking against known breach databases (e.g., Have I Been Pwned), implementing robust login rate limiting and IP throttling, using cryptographically secure session identifiers stored with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookie flags, invalidating sessions on logout and idle timeo
red with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookie flags, invalidating sessions on logout and idle timeouts, and keeping credentials out of source code by utilizing secrets management solutions.

section: A08:2025 - Software or Data Integrity Failures
text: ## A08:2025 - Software or Data Integrity Failures Software or Data Integrity Failures (ranked #8 in 2025) focuses on code and infrastructure that treats unverified or untrusted code or serialized objects as valid. A critical subset of this category is Insecure Deserialization (CWE-502). Applications often serialize complex objects into binary or text formats (such as Java native serialization or Python's pickle) and transmit or store them. When an application deserializes untrusted input without

When an application deserializes untrusted input without validation, an attacker can manipulate object structures to invoke arbitrary method chains (gadget chains), leading to Remote Code Execution (RCE), arbitrary file writes, or privilege escalation. Other vulnerabilities include unverified auto-update mechanisms downloading executable files without digital signature checks, trusting dynamic plugins or scripts loaded from unverified CDNs, and mass as

section: A08:2025 - Software or Data Integrity Failures

Prevention requires never accepting serialized objects from untrusted sources, preferring standard, safe data interchange formats like JSON or Protocol Buffers, implementing strict object filtering (e.g., Java ObjectInputFilter), signing and verifying digital signatures on all updates and bina

section: A08:2025 - Software or Data Integrity Failures

section: A09:2025 - Security Logging and Alerting Failures
text: ## A09:2025 - Security Logging and Alerting Failures Security Logging and Alerting Failures (ranked #9 in 2025, updated to place explicit emphasis on real-time alerting) addresses deficiencies in recording security events and detecting active intrusions. Without adequate logging and alerting, attacks cannot be detected, investigated, or contained, allowing attackers to maintain persistence, pivot laterally, and exfiltrate data undetected for months. Failures occur when auditable security events

section: A09:2025 - Security Logging and Alerting Failures
text: laterally, and exfiltrate data undetected for months. Failures occur when auditable security events (such as failed logins, access control denials, server-side validation errors, exception states, privilege escalations, and sensitive data exports) are not logged, when log entries omit crucial context (timestamps, user IDs, IP addresses), when logs are stored insecurely where attackers can tamper with or delete them, when log injection occurs due to unescaped user input in log messages, and when

section: A09:2025 - Security Logging and Alerting Failures

## A10:2025 - Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions is a brand-new category in the 2025 edition (ranked #10), consolidating weaknesses related to improper exception handling, unhandled error states, and insecure logic branching. When an application encounters unexpected inputs, network timeouts, resource exhaustion, or runtime errors, failing to handle these conditions securely can cause the application to crash, leak sensitive internals, or "fail open" — in

onditions securely can cause the application to crash, leak sensitive internals, or "fail open" — inadvertently bypassing security checks. Common vulnerabilities include "failing open" (CWE-636) where an exception during authentication or permission checking defaults to granting access instead of denying, verbose error messages (CWE-209) exposing stack traces, internal software versions, database structures, or physical file paths to attackers, unhandled NULL pointer dereferences (CWE-476) or un

structures, or physical file paths to attackers, unhandled NULL pointer dereferences (CWE-476) or uncaught exceptions leading to denial of service, improper handling of missing parameters (CWE-234), and generic catch-all blocks (`catch (Exception e) {}` or `except: pass`) that swallow critical errors and leave systems in inconsistent or vulnerable states. Prevention requires designing systems to always "fail secure" (defaulting to denial of access and safe aborts when errors occur), validating a

document_title: OWASP Path Traversal & Safe File Access Cheat Sheet
text: ## Introduction Path Traversal (also known as Directory Traversal or Dot-Dot-Slash attack) occurs when an application uses user-controllable input to construct file paths without proper sanitization or boundary verification. Attackers exploit this to read or write files outside the intended target directory, accessing sensitive source code, configuration files, system credentials, or overwriting application binaries.

document_title: OWASP Path Traversal & Safe File Access Cheat Sheet
text: ## Attack Vectors 1. **Dot-Dot-Slash Sequences:** Input containing `../../etc/passwd` or `..\..\windows\system32\config\sam`. 2. **URL and Unicode Encoding Bypass:** Patterns like `%2e%2e%2f`, `..%252f`, or null-byte injections (`%00`) in legacy platforms. 3. **Absolute Path Overwrites:** Passing `/etc/shadow` or `C:\boot.ini` directly into path join methods that overwrite the base root prefix.

document_title: OWASP Path Traversal & Safe File Access Cheat Sheet

# OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet Source: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html Retrieved: 2026-10-11 Author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series Team

## Introduction Secrets are credentials, API keys, tokens, private keys, connection strings, passwords, or any sensitive value used by an application to authenticate itself to external services or protect data. Mismanaged secrets are a leading cause of breaches — exposed secrets in repositories, configuration files, logs, or binary artifacts have resulted in some of the most significant cloud security incidents of the last decade.

## Core Principles of Secrets Management ### 1. Never Hardcode Secrets in Source Code Hardcoded secrets in source code violate CWE-798 and OWASP A07:2021 (Identification and Authentication Failures). Source code is frequently committed to version control, shared among teams, decompiled from binaries, or inadvertently exposed. **Vulnerable Java:** // CRITICALLY INSECURE — extractable by javap/jadx decompiler private static final String AWS_SECRET_KEY = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE_SECRET"; private stati
decompiler private static final String AWS_SECRET_KEY = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE_SECRET"; private static final String DB_PASSWORD = "RootAdmin_2026!"; **Vulnerable Python:** python

Restrict Secret Access with Least Privilege - Apply the principle of least privilege: each service or microservice should only have access to the secrets it strictly needs. - Use separate credentials for development, staging, and production environments. - Never share production credentials with developers for local development.

## Detecting Hardcoded Secrets Use static analysis tools as part of the CI/CD pipeline to automatically detect hardcoded secrets before code is merged: - **truffleHog** — scans Git history for high-entropy strings and regex-based secrets. - **detect-secrets** — Yelp's tool; integrates with pre-commit hooks. - **GitGuardian** — real-time monitoring of GitHub/GitLab commits for secret exposure. - **Semgrep** — rule-based SAST that supports custom secret patterns.

## Environment Variable Security When using environment variables: - Set them at the deployment/orchestration layer (e.g., Kubernetes secrets mounted as environment variables, AWS ECS task definitions, Docker secrets). - Never commit `.env` files containing real secrets to version control. Add `.env` to `.gitignore`. - Use `.env.example` (with placeholder values only) as a template.

## Secret Classification Classify secrets by sensitivity and handle accordingly: | Secret Type | Example | Storage Method | |---------------------|---------------------------------|---------------------------| | Database passwords | PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB creds | Secrets Manager / env var | | API keys | OpenAI, Stripe, AWS API keys | Secrets Manager / env var | | Private keys | TLS private key, SSH key | Key Vault / HSM | | JWT signing secrets | HS256 secret key | Secrets Manager | | OAuth c

## Version Control Hygiene If a secret has ever been committed to a Git repository, assume it is compromised — even after removal via `git rm` or `git rebase`. The commit history retains the exposed value. Required remediation steps: 1. Immediately invalidate/rotate the exposed secret. 2. Use `git-filter-repo` or BFG Repo Cleaner to remove the secret from all history. 3. Force-push to all remotes and notify all collaborators to reclone. 4. and notify all collaborators to reclone. 4. Audit access logs for the period during which the secret was exposed.

document_title: OWASP Secure File Upload Cheat Sheet
text: ## Introduction Allowing users to upload files is a powerful capability but introduces critical risks if files are executed on the host server, stored in publicly accessible paths, or permitted to exhaust server storage resources.

document_title: OWASP Secure File Upload Cheat Sheet
text: ## Vulnerabilities and Threat Scenarios 1. **Remote Code Execution (RCE):** Uploading executable scripts (`.php`, `.jsp`, `.py`, `.exe`, `.cgi`) to web roots where web servers execute them on request. 2. **Denial of Service (DoS):** Uploading excessively large files or decompression bombs ("zip bombs") to exhaust server memory or disk storage. 3. **Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS):** Uploading HTML, SVG, or PDF files containing malicious JavaScript that executes when viewed in a browser context

document_title: OWASP Secure File Upload Cheat Sheet
text: ML, SVG, or PDF files containing malicious JavaScript that executes when viewed in a browser context. 4. **MIME-Type Spoofing:** Supplying a forged `Content-Type: image/jpeg` header for an uploaded binary payload.

Define an explicit allow-list of safe extensions (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.pdf`). Verify the file magic numbers / binary signature, not merely the filename extension or HTTP `Content-Type` header. ### 2. Randomize Stored Filenames Never store files on disk using the original client-provided filename. Generate an independent random UUID or cryptographically strong identifier. #

text: # OWASP Security Misconfiguration Prevention Cheat Sheet Source: https://owasp.org/Top10/A05_2021-Security_Misconfiguration/ Retrieved: 2026-10-12 Author: OWASP Top 10 Team Topic: Security Misconfiguration & Hardening

## Introduction Security misconfiguration is commonly found in web applications where developers or system administrators fail to implement secure configuration defaults across all layers of the application stack, including network services, web servers, databases, and application runtimes.

## Attack Scenarios and High-Risk Patterns 1. **Enabled Debug Mode in Production:** Running frameworks with `debug=True` (e.g., Flask Werkzeug interactive debugger, Django DEBUG mode, or Spring Boot DevTools) exposes interactive consoles, secret keys, environment variables, and full stack traces. 2. **Default Accounts and Unchanged Passwords:** Deploying databases, message queues, or administrative panels with default passwords enabled. 3. **Missing Security Headers:** Failing to emit modern bro

e panels with default passwords enabled. 3. **Missing Security Headers:** Failing to emit modern browser security headers allows cross-origin data theft, MIME confusion attacks, and clickjacking. 4. **Directory Listing Enabled:** Web servers serving directory indexes when default index files are missing, exposing sensitive source files and backups.

## Hardening Guidance & Mitigation ### 1. Disable Debug Runtimes in Production Ensure production entry points strictly read boolean flags from verified environment variables and default to safe production configurations. import os
# Unsafe:
# app.run(debug=True)

# Safe: FLASK_DEBUG = os.getenv("FLASK_DEBUG", "0") == "1" app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=FLASK_DEBUG) ### 2. Implement Essential HTTP Security Headers All API and web responses should include: - `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'` - `X-Frame-Options: DENY` - `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` - `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` - `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` ### 3. Automated Hardening Checklist - Remove unused features, e

y: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` ### 3. Automated Hardening Checklist - Remove unused features, endpoints, sample files, and documentation in production builds. - Configure error handlers to return generic error identifiers without internal system disclosures. - Regularly audit cloud buckets (AWS S3, GCP Buckets) for accidental public read permissions.

text: ## Introduction Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) occurs when a web application fetches a remote resource without validating the user-supplied URL. An attacker can coerce the application to send crafted requests to unexpected destinations, typically bypassing network firewalls to target internal cloud metadata services, loopback interfaces, or intranets.

document_title: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
text: ## Introduction Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is a type of injection attack in which malicious scripts are injected into otherwise benign and trusted websites. XSS attacks occur when an attacker uses a web application to send malicious code, generally in the form of a browser side script, to a different end user.

document_title: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
text: ## Types of XSS - **Stored XSS:** The malicious input is permanently stored on the target servers (e.g. database, comment field, forum post) and delivered to victims when requesting the stored information. - **Reflected XSS:** The malicious payload is reflected off a web application into the user's browser via error messages, search results, or URL parameters. - **DOM-based XSS:** The vulnerability exists in client-side code rather than server-side code, where client JavaScript reads data from a

document_title: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
text: ## Content Security Policy (CSP) Implement a robust Content Security Policy (CSP) HTTP response header. CSP provides defense-in-depth by restricting where scripts can be loaded from and disabling the execution of inline scripts (`unsafe-inline`) and `eval()`.
